name: FixMe filter

card.summary: An Instagram filter that let users draw surgical-style markings on their own face, mimicking how a plastic surgeon marks areas for planned improvement.
card.note: Facebook banned cosmetic-procedure filters in October 2019.

quick.overview:
FixMe was a third-party Instagram filter that let people annotate a selfie with marks like those a plastic surgeon draws before an operation, highlighting areas they might want to change.

It relates to appearance as a way of visualising what a person might want to improve, and it became part of a public debate on filters and cosmetic surgery, including the term Snapchat dysmorphia. Few details about the filter itself are documented.
quick.how: Users opened the filter on Instagram and marked up their own face to indicate features they wanted altered, then shared the image.
quick.risks: The filter itself carried no physical risk. It was criticised in public debate about filters and body image, and Facebook banned cosmetic-procedure and distortion filters in October 2019.

lead: FixMe was an Instagram filter that allowed users to annotate their face with areas for surgical improvement, in the way a plastic surgeon might mark a patient with a pen. [1] Wikipedia does not name its creator or launch date.

It is mentioned in discussion of Snapchat dysmorphia, a term coined by cosmetic doctor Tijion Esho for patients who ask surgeons for procedures that mimic filtered images, such as a narrower nose, bigger eyes or fuller lips. [1] After public controversy over cosmetic-procedure filters, Facebook banned them and all 'distortion' filters in October 2019. [1]

chain: Notes what they might want to change
angle.text: The filter gave a way to visualise features someone might want to change, which some people use as a starting point when thinking about procedures.

paras: The filter let users mark their face with 'areas for surgical improvement'. [1]

Cosmetic-procedure filters drew public controversy and were banned by Facebook in October 2019. [1] Snapchat dysmorphia, coined by Tijion Esho, describes people seeking surgery to resemble filtered images; Wikipedia says the link to filters is described but not established as causal. [1]
